newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Maluf kicks off Brazil president race 2 yrs early.
newsitem.headline: Maluf kicks off Brazil president race 2 yrs early.

text.p: A tub-thumping attack on the Brazilian government by Paulo Maluf, Sao Paulo's irrepressibly ambitious mayor, has kicked off Brazil's 1998 presidential race two years early, analysts and politicians said.

But Maluf, who hogged the headlines on Wednesday after lambasting President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election dream in a speech in Congress, remains an outside candidate with a thirst for power that may never be fully quenched, they said.

"He is the most ambitious politician in Brazil today," said Dep. Luiz Gushiken of the left-wing Workers Party who campaigned in vain against Maluf's hand-chosen successor in Sao Paulo's municipal race this month. "Expect everything from this man."

Maluf has never fully shed the stigma of being the defeated official candidate of Brazil's dictatorship in the first presidential elections of civil rule in 1985, going on to lose races for the state governorship and town hall of Sao Paulo.

Renowned for his undentable self-belief, Maluf finally won the Sao Paulo mayorship in 1992 and his program of high-profile public works gave his protege, Celso Pitta, a resounding 57 percent of this month's vote. Opponents point to Sao Paulo's exploding municipal debt as the other side of the Maluf coin.

Although he has not explicitly said he will run in 1998, Maluf has repeatedly hinted he wants to succeed Cardoso. "He's obsessed with the presidency and at 65 he must make his move now," said Carlos Lopes of analysts Santafe Ideias.

Maluf is considered the biggest threat to Cardoso's plan to rewrite the electoral laws and stand again for an unprecedented second term in 1998. His first priority appears to be to unite the Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB) -- over which he has sway but not control -- against re-election.

In a speech on Tuesday to a Chamber of Deputies committee mulling re-election, Maluf said Cardoso's plan for a second term was unethical and blamed his government for everything from unemployment to outbreaks of killer diseases in baby clinics.
"The government is hostage to re-election...Nothing is being done in this country because re-election is everything," he told the meeting, which was jammed with onlookers and the media.
Maluf also said he would challenge in the Supreme Federal Tribunal any calling of an extraordinary session of Congress to deal with re-election, as is expected for January.

But most observers say Maluf is unlikely to match the government's bargaining power to turn Congress against re-election. He would then stand little chance against Cardoso, who has public opinion and big campaign funders on his side.
Already, there are suggestions Maluf may back down from his presidential push and settle instead for a crack at the Sao Paulo state governorship.
Analyst Carlos Setti of Goes e Consultores said Maluf may even help Cardoso's re-election bid by rallying supporters of the government behind the president.
"Maluf's rejection rate remains very high," Setti said. "He will polarize Brazil between those in favor and those against." -- Brasilia newsroom 5561 2230358 (c) Reuters Limited 1996
